MD 8.3 Evaluation
                        Decision Documentation for Reactive Inspection
                            (Deterministic and Risk Criteria Analyzed)

PLANT:                   EVENT DATE:             DETERMINISTIC CRITERIA EVALUATION DATE:
Palisades                09/03/2026              09/03/2026, 09/11/2026

On 9/3/2026, Palisades Nuclear Plant was performing fuel moves in Mode 6 as part of their restart
operations. A fuel assembly was being manipulated and had difficulty seating in its designated
core position and location. Per the licensee’s fuel movement procedure, a conversation was held
between Reactor Engineering and the fuel move team to perform a deviation to the prescribed
fuel move sheets to rotate the assembly. After rotating the bundle, the fuel handling crew
attempted to seat it in its designated core location again. After using available verification tools to
ensure the fuel assembly was seated, the fuel handlers un-grappled the bundle. After the load
was removed from the fuel handling machine, the fuel assembly proceeded to tip over and fall. It
came to rest at an angle on the core shroud and core plate. The licensee entered AOP-34, “Fuel
Handling Accident,” and completed all actions, including a stop to all work, an evacuation of all
workers from containment, and closure of containment.

On September 3, 2026, a group of regional branch chiefs and subject matter experts with
specialties in plant operations and the regional Senior Risk Analysts were convened to discuss
the circumstances surrounding the event. At that time, the group decided to reconvene if/when
additional information became available that would help inform decision-making related to the
deterministic questions. On September 11, 2026, the group reconvened to go over additional
information related to the sequence of events from additional inspections, evaluations, and
interviews after the event.

Y/N                                      DETERMINISTIC CRITERIA

N         1. Involved operations that exceeded, or were not included in, the design bases of the
          facility

          Remarks: Following evaluation of the event and review of the design basis events in
          Chapter 14 of the FSAR, it is believed that the event is bounded by Section 14.19
          (dropped fuel assembly).

N         2. Involved a major deficiency in design, construction, or operation having potential
          generic safety implications

          Remarks: No generic safety implications have been identified.

N         3. Led to a significant loss of integrity of the fuel, primary coolant pressure boundary, or
          primary containment boundary of a nuclear reactor

          Remarks: Currently, based on visual inspections, radiological monitoring, and chemical
          sampling of the water in the reactor cavity, the fuel rods within the fuel assembly do not
          show indications of any damage. The tipping of this assembly does not appear, based
          on visual inspection, to have damaged any other fuel assemblies currently loaded into
          the core. There are some indications that the fuel assembly caused damage to the core
     shroud as it fell; however, the impact of this is still being evaluated by the licensee.
    Current monitoring of radiological and primary coolant system conditions indicates that
    any potential damage to the core shroud or core plate has not impacted the barrier
    function of the primary coolant system.

N   4. Led to the loss of a safety function or multiple failures in systems used to mitigate an
    actual event

    Remarks: There was not a loss of safety function or mitigating system failures.

N   5. Involved possible adverse generic implications

    Remarks: No adverse generic safety implications were identified.

N   6. Involved significant unexpected system interactions

    Remarks: No unexpected system interactions occurred.

N   7. Involved repetitive failures or events involving safety-related equipment or
    deficiencies in operations

    Remarks: No repetitive failures or deficiencies in operation of safety-related equipment
    occurred.

Y   8. Involved questions or concerns pertaining to licensee operational performance

    Remarks: When the licensee initially attempted to seat this fuel assembly in the
    designated position and location, they did not get indications of a full seat. Per the
    fuel movement procedure, and after a conversation between the Reactor Engineering
    team and fuel handling team in the field, Reactor Engineering wrote a deviation form
    to move the assembly to the fuel upender, rotate it, re-grapple and move it back to its
    designated core location. However, when attempting to set the fuel assembly into the
    fuel upender, it wouldn’t properly fit back in. Another deviation was written to rotate the
    fuel assembly in the mast of the refueling machine in the core. When attempting to place
    the assembly in the designated core location a second time, while verifying available
    indications, extra weight was noted on the refueling machine grapple by one individual.
    The grappler was again re-lowered until the weight indicated the expected value for the
    fuel assembly being seated. At this point, the licensee verified other indications for a full
    seat. When the fuel handling team unhooked the grappler, the fuel assembly tipped
    over.

    The regional review team and senior management discussed this question in detail.
    Additional information reviewed from the licensee’s documented fact-finding process
    raised concerns regarding operational performance. Based on the information provided
    in interview statements, it appears the fuel handling team followed the fuel movement
    procedure, including the deviation process. However, there were multiple opportunities
    for individuals to better demonstrate use of their human performance tools for
    questioning attitude and stop when unsure throughout the event. Prior to the fuel
    assembly tipping over, personnel encountered a series of abnormal conditions: they




                                         2
          required approximately 50 pounds more force than expected to remove the assembly
         from the upender, noted rubbing or interference, were unable to properly fit the
         assembly back into the upender, experienced repeated difficulty seating the assembly
         in the core, and observed abnormal refueling machine load indications. These
         observations prompted questions about how these abnormal conditions were evaluated
         and whether they were sufficiently understood before fuel movement continued.
         As a result, it was determined this question should be answered ‘Yes’.

RISK ANALYSIS BY: N/A                                      DATE: N/A

Brief Description of the Basis for the Assessment (may include assumptions, calculations,
references, peer review, or comparison with licensee’s results): The SRA determined available
quantitative risk tools and methods were not appropriate for the evaluation of this event.
Therefore, it would be more appropriate to use the deterministic criteria in this form to evaluate the
risk of the event.

The estimated conditional core damage probability (CCDP) is ___________________ and places
the risk in the range of a _______________ and ____________________ inspection.

  APPROPRIATE, DOCUMENT THE RESPONSE DECISION TO THE EVENT OR CONDITION,
  AND THE BASIS FOR THAT DECISION

  DECISION AND DETAILS OF THE BASIS FOR THE DECISION:

  A risk evaluation was not performed because no applicable risk model exists for this condition.
  Management concluded that inspection follow-up is warranted and can initially be conducted
  through the baseline inspection program. Information gathered during baseline inspection may
  warrant reconsideration of whether a reactive inspection is appropriate. Any new information will
  be re-evaluated as necessary to ensure the assessment remains accurate.

Brief Description of the Significant Event or Degraded Condition: On 9/3/2026, Palisades Nuclear
Plant was performing fuel moves in Mode 6 as part of their restart operations. A fuel assembly
was being manipulated and had difficulty seating in its designated core position and location. Per
the licensee’s fuel movement procedure, a conversation was held between Reactor Engineering
and the fuel move team to perform a deviation to the prescribed fuel move sheets to rotate the
assembly. After rotating the bundle, the fuel handling crew attempted to seat it in its designated
core location again. After using available verification tools to ensure the fuel assembly was
seated, the fuel handlers un-grappled the bundle. After the load was removed from the fuel
handling machine, the fuel assembly proceeded to tip over and fall. It came to rest at an angle on
the core shroud and core plate. The licensee entered AOP-34, “Fuel Handling Accident,” and
completed all actions, including a stop to all work, an evacuation of all workers from containment,
and closure of containment.

    Remarks: Based on the information provided in interview statements, it appears the fuel
    handling team followed the fuel movement procedure, including the deviation process.
